candidates.quote: A thousand words leave not the same / Deep print as does a single deed.
candidates.author: Henrik Ibsen
candidates.locator: Second Act, the villagers’ spokesman asking Brand to be their priest; Everyman’s Library edition (J. M. Dent, 1915; 1951 reprint), p. 51, read in the archive.org scan brand00ibse. Calendar For Life carries an untraced prose paraphrase (A thousand words will not leave so deep an impression as one deed); this is Garrett’s printed verse. Herford’s 1894 rendering of the same couplet is: A thousand speeches brand / Less deeply than one dint of deed.
candidates.whyThisMonth: The month’s blurb in two lines of verse: the day is changed by the one thing done, not by the thousand things said about it.
candidates.speaker: The Man

candidates.quote: Our life is March weather, savage and serene in one hour.
candidates.author: Ralph Waldo Emerson
candidates.locator: Lecture IV, Montaigne; or, the Skeptic (Phillips, Sampson and Company, 1850), about two thirds through, the sentence before We go forth austere, dedicated; read in place in the Wikisource text of Representative Men.
candidates.whyThisMonth: A March line for March: it admits that resolve swings with the hour, which is the whole case for leaning on habit rather than on mood.

candidates.quote: The maturity of man—that means, to have reacquired the seriousness that one had as a child at play.
candidates.author: Friedrich Nietzsche
candidates.locator: Chapter IV, Apophthegms and Interludes, section 94; read in the Project Gutenberg text (etext 4363), a reprint of Zimmern’s translation as issued in the Levy Complete Works (1909 to 1913). Calendar For Life carries this as Heraclitus (Man is most nearly himself when he achieves the seriousness of a child at play); no Heraclitus fragment reads so, and the sentence is Nietzsche’s. The nearest fragment, B52, is about time as a child playing.
candidates.whyThisMonth: It names what practice is for: not grim effort but the absorbed seriousness a child brings to a game, earned back on purpose.

candidates.quote: I did not care what it was all about. All I wanted to know was how to live in it. Maybe if you found out how to live in it you learned from that what it was all about.
candidates.author: Ernest Hemingway
candidates.locator: Book II, chapter 14, Jake Barnes awake at night in Pamplona (Charles Scribner’s Sons, 1926); read in place in the Project Gutenberg text (etext 67138). Hemingway’s Old Man and the Sea line is already in the carry for July, so this would be a second Hemingway in the year, not a third.
candidates.whyThisMonth: Practice before theory: learn how to live the day and the meaning may follow, which is permission to start the work without having settled what it is all for.
candidates.speaker: Jake Barnes

candidates.quote: Eternity is in love with the productions of time.
candidates.author: William Blake
candidates.work: The Marriage of Heaven and Hell
candidates.locator: Proverbs of Hell, plate 7, the tenth proverb; read in place in the Project Gutenberg text (etext 45315), where it stands just before The busy bee has no time for sorrow.
candidates.whyThisMonth: It tells the maker at the desk that the small thing finished today is exactly what the large scheme of things is fond of.

candidates.quote: He who reads much and travels much sees and knows a great deal.
candidates.author: Miguel de Cervantes
candidates.locator: Part II, chapter XXV, Don Quixote on seeing Master Pedro’s divining ape; read in the Project Gutenberg text of Ormsby (etext 996). In the edition the words follow ‘Now I declare,’ said Don Quixote, so the he is lower case there and the capital is the card’s. The comic setting is worth a note: he says it while being taken in by a fraud. Calendar For Life’s wording (reads much and walks much, sees much and knows much) is a literal version of el que lee mucho y anda mucho, vee mucho y sabe mucho that I could not trace to a named translation.
candidates.whyThisMonth: Two plain habits, reading and going about on foot, offered as the whole curriculum.
candidates.speaker: Don Quixote

candidates.quote: Yet such is oft the course of deeds that move the wheels of the world: small hands do them because they must, while the eyes of the great are elsewhere.
candidates.author: J. R. R. Tolkien
candidates.locator: Book II, chapter 2, The Council of Elrond (George Allen and Unwin, 1954); wording as given by WIST (wist.info/tolkien-jrr/52014) and Tolkien Gateway, the printed page not opened. Calendar For Life carries a loose paraphrase marked after Tolkien (It is not the strong who survive, nor the wise, but the small hands that do the work); this is the sentence behind it. Mind the cap: three Tolkien lines already sit in the carry for months 4, 10 and 11.
candidates.whyThisMonth: The work that matters is mostly done unwatched, by people who simply do what the day requires, and that is a steadying thing to hear before anyone else is up.
candidates.speaker: Elrond

candidates.quote: I have finished a monument more lasting than bronze and loftier than the Pyramids’ royal pile, one that no wasting rain, no furious north wind can destroy, or the countless chain of years and the ages’ flight.
candidates.author: Horace
candidates.locator: Book III, ode 30, lines 1 to 5, the opening sentence (Exegi monumentum aere perennius); Bennett’s prose translation in the Loeb Classical Library Odes and Epodes (Heinemann and Macmillan, 1914), wording as given by WIST (wist.info/horace/72450), which dates it 1912; the Loeb page itself was not opened. Calendar For Life’s wording (I have raised a monument more lasting than bronze) matched no named translation I could find.
candidates.whyThisMonth: A writer looking at three books of finished poems and saying what the daily labour came to: the one honest reward of discipline is the thing made.

candidates.quote: And we should consider every day lost on which we have not danced at least once.
candidates.author: Friedrich Nietzsche
candidates.locator: Third Part, On Old and New Tablets, section 23, in Kaufmann’s translation in The Portable Nietzsche (Viking, 1954). The section is confirmed in Common’s 1909 translation on Project Gutenberg (etext 1998: And lost be the day to us in which a measure hath not been danced). Kaufmann’s wording is from memory and secondary quotation; every archive.org copy is lending-locked, so his page was not opened and the verifier should find it. An alternate to 03-cfl-03, not a companion: one Nietzsche at most.
candidates.whyThisMonth: A daily rule with no grimness in it: the habit worth keeping is the one that gets the body moving and glad once before night.
candidates.speaker: Zarathustra

candidates.quote: I can resist everything except temptation.
candidates.author: Oscar Wilde
candidates.locator: First Act, Lord Darlington to Lady Windermere, following I couldn’t help it; first performed 1892, published by Elkin Mathews and John Lane, 1893; read in place in the Project Gutenberg text (etext 790).
candidates.whyThisMonth: A month of discipline needs one day that laughs at it, and the joke is also an accurate description of where the difficulty lies.
candidates.speaker: Lord Darlington

candidates.quote: There is only one recipe for a best seller and it is a very simple one. You have to get the reader to turn over the page.
candidates.author: Ian Fleming
candidates.locator: Books and Bookmen, vol. 8, no. 8, May 1963, pp. 14 to 19; wording read in the Literary Hub reprint of the essay (lithub.com/ian-fleming-explains-how-to-write-a-thriller). A version of the piece ran earlier in Show, August 1962, which I did not see. Calendar For Life runs the two sentences together with a colon; the essay does not. Fame is modest: it is the sentence the essay is known by, no more. Fleming’s Casino Royale line is already in the carry for September.
candidates.whyThisMonth: A working writer on the work of writing, with the craft reduced to one test that can be applied to today’s page.

candidates.quote: You can’t get away from yourself by moving from one place to another.
candidates.author: Ernest Hemingway
candidates.locator: Book I, chapter 2, Jake Barnes to Robert Cohn, who wants to go to South America (Charles Scribner’s Sons, 1926); read in place in the Project Gutenberg text (etext 67138). An alternate to 03-cfl-04, the weaker of the two for this theme: one Hemingway at most.
candidates.whyThisMonth: The work of becoming cannot be outsourced to a change of scene: whatever is to be mended gets mended here, by the person who woke up this morning.
candidates.speaker: Jake Barnes
